name: Octinoxate

lead: Octinoxate is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB, the burning part of sunlight. It is common in sunscreens, SPF lip balms and cosmetics, and people use it to avoid sunburn, uneven tone and sun-related aging.

It absorbs UVB (about 290-320 nm) and dissipates the energy as heat. Its appearance benefit comes through sun protection generally. Lab studies have reported hormone-like activity and trials show it enters the bloodstream, and in 2025 the EU's SCCS concluded it is safe up to 10%.

paras: It is applied as a daily sunscreen or in SPF lip balm and makeup. Sunlight can convert it to a form that absorbs less, so it is usually blended with other filters.

Reported concerns are endocrine activity in cell and animal studies, systemic absorption and coral reef effects; human clinical harm has not been shown in the studies listed. Hawaii and Palau restrict it. Allowed levels are 7.5% in the US and 10% in the EU.

chain: Fewer sunspots and wrinkles over time
angle.text: Octinoxate absorbs UVB light, so there is less sun damage, fewer sunspots and less wrinkling over time. Its UVB absorption is well characterised; the appearance benefit comes from sun protection generally.

lead: Octinoxate (octyl methoxycinnamate, ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, OMC) is an organic UVB filter used in sunscreens, lip balms and cosmetics with SPF claims [1][2]. It absorbs UVB with a peak near 310 nm and is typically combined with other filters [2]. For appearance, its role is sun protection: sunscreen helps prevent sunburn and, according to the US FDA, may reduce the risk of early skin aging [3], and Wikipedia describes daily broad-spectrum sunscreen as slowing or temporarily preventing wrinkles, dark spots and sagging [4].

Octinoxate is described as the most common UVB-absorbing active ingredient in sunscreens, with maximum permitted concentrations of 7.5% in the US and Canada, 10% in the EU and Australia and 20% in Japan [2][4]. It has drawn regulatory and scientific attention for endocrine activity seen in laboratory and animal studies, for systemic absorption in humans, and for restrictions on sunscreens containing it in places such as Hawaii and Palau on environmental grounds [1][2][4].

The European Commission's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) published an opinion in June 2025 concluding it is safe at up to 10% in cosmetics, according to both encyclopedia sources [1][2]. A 2025 toxicology review concluded that a mode-of-action approach supports a lack of carcinogenic potential for six organic UV filters [5].
infobox: Octyl methoxycinnamate, ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, Eusolex 2292, Uvinul MC80
Colourless to pale-yellow oily liquid, insoluble in water [2]

paras: Octinoxate is described as the most common UVB-absorbing active ingredient in sunscreens and is often combined with oxybenzone and titanium dioxide [2]. It appears on US labels for lip balms and SPF products, often alongside avobenzone, octisalate and octocrylene [6]. Wikipedia also notes use in products meant to reduce the appearance of scars [2].

Sunscreen relevance. The FDA says sunscreen helps prevent sunburn and may reduce the risks of skin cancer and early skin aging, that SPF reflects protection against UVB, and that broad-spectrum sunscreens protect against both UVA and UVB; octinoxate itself is a UVB filter and is therefore usually paired with UVA filters [3][2]. Research has also examined photoprotection as part of melasma treatment [7].

It is a colourless to pale-yellow oily ester of methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethylhexanol that is insoluble in water [1][2]. One synthesis route is cross metathesis of trans-anethole with 2-ethylhexyl acrylate [2]. Under sunlight it isomerises from the E to the Z form, reducing UV absorption, which is why stabilisers are used [1][2]. A review of photostability discusses why filter photostability matters to human safety [8]. Inorganic filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, reviewed separately, are the main alternatives [9].

A 2001 study of UV screens reported estrogenic activity in cultured cells and in rat experiments for several filters [10]. A 2004 review updated findings on endocrine activity and developmental toxicity of cosmetic UV filters [11]. In a human study, researchers measured systemic absorption of octinoxate, benzophenone-3 and 4-methylbenzylidene camphor after whole-body application alongside reproductive hormone levels [12], and a later study measured filters in plasma and urine after repeated application [13]. A 2020 JAMA trial found octinoxate and other ingredients in plasma after sunscreen use; the FDA has said that this shows absorption and has requested more safety data, but has not concluded the ingredients are unsafe [14][4]. A 2017 review discussed possible neurotoxic effects of sunscreen ingredients, mainly from laboratory work [15]. A 2023 study combined in vivo and in vitro data to examine octinoxate as a potential thyroid hormone disruptor [16], and a 2025 review appraised the risk of octinoxate and oxybenzone for people with polycystic ovary syndrome [17].

Wikipedia lists a rat study in which octinoxate reduced postoperative peritoneal adhesions, a 2000 study that linked it to toxicity in mouse cells at concentrations below typical sunscreen levels, another study that found little skin penetration, and a 2017 report of genotoxic effects of its isomers in laboratory conditions [2]. Grokipedia states that causal links to human health outcomes lack large-scale clinical data [1].

Reviews have examined effects of octinoxate and other sunscreen ingredients on coral reefs [18]. Wikipedia reports that Hawaii banned sales of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018, and that Key West, the US Virgin Islands, Bonaire and Palau have also restricted such ingredients; Palau's law, enacted in 2018 and effective in 2020, covers octinoxate and nine other chemicals [4][2]. "Reef-safe" labels are not regulated [4].

The EU allows up to 10% in cosmetics and placed octinoxate on its 2019 priority list of potential endocrine disruptors before the June 2025 SCCS opinion found it safe at up to 10% [2]. In the US, sunscreen is regulated as an over-the-counter drug, and since 2019 the FDA has sorted UV filters into those generally recognized as safe and effective, those not, and those needing more data; Wikipedia says only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were classified as safe and effective as of 2021 [4].

Human research is mainly pharmacokinetic. A phase 1 programme enrolled 72 participants and measured absorption of sunscreen ingredients including octinoxate [19][14], and a 2004 study measured absorption and reproductive hormones [12]. A 1,000-person European photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients generally [20]. A controlled trial reported that a high-SPF sunscreen prevented UVB-induced immunosuppression in humans [21]. No trial found tests octinoxate alone for appearance outcomes.
